results.construction: Tap lattice point (3,-2): 3 right, 2 down (quadrant IV).

predicates.why: Fires on tapping (-2,3), the reversed pair, which is distinct from the target. This is the signature of treating (a,b) as the unordered {a,b}.

results.construction: Tap lattice point (-3,1): 3 left, 1 up (quadrant II).

predicates.why: Fires on tapping (1,-3), the reversed pair, which is distinct from the target. This is what a student who ignores order would plot.

results.construction: Tap lattice point (-3,-4): 3 left, 4 down (quadrant III).

predicates.why: Fires on tapping (-4,-3), the reversed pair, which is distinct from the target. This is what a student who ignores order would plot.

results.construction: Tap the four ordered pairs with first coordinate from X and second from Y: (2,4), (2,0), (-1,4), (-1,0). This is exactly |X|·|Y| = 4 pairs, with no decoys tapped.

predicates.why: The predicate fires when the student taps (4,2), (4,-1), (0,2), (0,-1), which is Y×X. A student who thinks X×Y and Y×X are the same set would build exactly this, using Y's elements as first coordinates. The sets are not symmetric here (2,4 vs 4,2), so the swap is detectable. A plain slip in reading the order could also produce it, but it is the most direct signature of this misconception.

results.construction: Tap all 6 ordered pairs with first coordinate from {4,0} and second from {4,5,-2}: (4,4), (4,5), (4,-2), (0,4), (0,5), (0,-2). Set sizes 2 and 3 are within limits.

predicates.why: Firing construction: tap the 6 pairs of the swapped product: (4,4), (5,4), (-2,4), (4,0), (5,0), (-2,0). The student treats the order of the sets as irrelevant and builds the product in the other order. This is the typical product-order-irrelevant error. Only (4,4) is in both products, so the reversal is clearly visible.

results.construction: Tap all 9 pairs of X×Y: (-1,2), (-1,4), (-1,6), (1,2), (1,4), (1,6), (2,2), (2,4), (2,6). Both sets have 3 numbers, within the 2–4 limit.

predicates.why: The predicate fires when the student taps the Y×X pairs, such as (2,-1), (4,1) and (6,2), instead of the X×Y pairs. That is what a student who writes the pair with the Y element first would build. The book/student wording in the misconception is a different context, but the error is the same. (2,2) is in both products, which doesn't change this.
